links.title: Fusion needs tunnelling

sideA.context: QM: particle of energy $E$ below a rectangular barrier of height $V_0$ and width $L$, with $\kappa L\gg1$

sideB.context: Astro: two nuclei $Z_1,Z_2$ with reduced mass $m_r$ and relative energy $E\ll$ Coulomb barrier, in a plasma of temperature $T$

map: $\kappa(r)=\sqrt{2m_r\,(V_C(r)-E)}/\hbar$ with $V_C=Z_1Z_2e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0r$, integrated from the turning point $r_t$ to the nuclear radius
$Z_1Z_2e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)-E$, which varies with $r$ (a sloping barrier, not a rectangle)
links.regime: The WKB form $e^{-2\int\kappa\,dx}$ is valid when $\kappa L\gg1$ and $\kappa$ varies slowly. For pp, $E_G=m_pc^2(\pi\alpha)^2\approx 493$ keV, but the Sun's core has only $k_BT\approx 1.3$ keV at $1.5\times10^7$ K, so the Gamow exponent is large and the rate is tiny but non-zero. The prefactor $16E(V_0-E)/V_0^2$ is replaced by the nuclear $S$-factor.
links.experiment: The pp-chain rate is $\propto\int e^{-E/k_BT}e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}dE$, peaked at the Gamow energy $E_0=(E_G(k_BT/2)^2)^{1/3}\approx 5.9$ keV, where the tunnelling factor is $e^{-9.1}\approx 10^{-4}$. Accelerator experiments (LUNA) measure cross sections $\sigma=S(E)e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}/E$ at keV energies.
links.intuition: The same exponential suppression by a forbidden region: the wave function decays as $e^{-\kappa x}$ inside. In the bridge the barrier is a rectangle; in the star it is the Coulomb tail, so $\kappa$ must be integrated.
links.exam: Nuclear Furnace: Gamow peak and temperature dependence of the rate; Tunneling Bridge: $T\approx e^{-2\kappa L}$ estimates.
links.why: The same exponential suppression by a forbidden region: the wave function decays as $e^{-\kappa x}$ inside. In the bridge the barrier is a rectangle; in the star it is the Coulomb tail, so $\kappa$ must be integrated.

links.title: The STM reads the density of states

sideA.context: QM: electron of energy $E$ tunnelling through a vacuum gap of width $d$ with work function $\phi$ ($V_0-E=\phi$)

sideB.context: Metals: sample as a free-electron gas at $T\ll T_F$, probed by a tip at small bias $U$

map: $I/U$ (tunnel conductance), times the number of available initial states
work function of tip/sample, typically $4$ to $5$ eV
all occupied sample states within $eU$ of $E_F$: weight $\nu_s(E_F)\,eU$
links.regime: Valid for small bias ($eU\ll\phi$) and low temperature so that only states at $E_F$ matter. For $\phi=4.5$ eV, $\kappa\approx1.09\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$, so the current drops by $e^{-2.17}\approx0.11$, about one decade, per Ångstrom of extra distance.
links.experiment: An STM at constant current follows the surface corrugation with sub-picometre vertical resolution; sweeping $U$ gives $dI/dU\propto\nu(eU)$, the local density of states. Typical currents: nA at $d\approx5$ Å.
links.intuition: Tunnelling probability supplies the extreme distance sensitivity (exponential), the electron gas supplies how many electrons can tunnel (Pauli: only filled states below $E_F$, empty states above).
links.exam: Tunneling Bridge STM side quest; Fermi Sea: free-electron $\nu(E)$.
links.tex: T\sim e^{-2\kappa d},\quad \kappa=\frac{\sqrt{2m\phi}}{\hbar}\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ I\propto U\,\nu_s(E_F)\,e^{-2\kappa d},\quad \nu(E)=\frac{V}{2\pi^2}\Big(\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\Big)^{3/2}\sqrt{E}
links.why: Tunnelling probability supplies the extreme distance sensitivity (exponential), the electron gas supplies how many electrons can tunnel (Pauli: only filled states below $E_F$, empty states above).

links.title: Box states become the Fermi sea

sideA.context: QM: free particle of mass $m$ in a cubic box of side $a$ with hard walls (or periodic boundary conditions)

sideB.context: Metals: $N$ non-interacting electrons in volume $V=L^3$ at $T=0$, periodic boundary conditions

links.regime: Needs non-interacting fermions, $T\ll T_F$ and $k$-points dense enough to replace the sum by an integral (macroscopic $L$). For copper, $n=8.49\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ gives $k_F=1.36\times10^{10}$ m$^{-1}$ and $E_F=7.0$ eV, $T_F=8.2\times10^4$ K.
links.experiment: Fermi energies of metals are read off from photoemission and de Haas-van Alphen experiments (few eV up to 10 eV for simple metals); the free-electron $k_F$ matches the Fermi-surface radius of Na, K, Cu to within a few percent.
links.intuition: A solid is a gigantic box; the Pauli principle fills it from the bottom, two per orbital level, so even at $T=0$ electrons carry huge kinetic energy.
links.exam: Free-electron gas problems: derive $k_F$, $E_F$, $\nu(E_F)$ from state counting.
links.why: A solid is a gigantic box; the Pauli principle fills it from the bottom, two per orbital level, so even at $T=0$ electrons carry huge kinetic energy.

links.title: The same Fermi gas, three courses

sideA.context: Metals: degenerate electrons ($T\ll T_F$) held in the solid by the positive ion lattice

sideB.context: White dwarf / degenerate stellar core: degenerate electrons held by gravity, ions provide the mass

map: gravity of the ions (the electrons are nearly massless to gravity)
$E_F\sim 0.1$ MeV for $n_e\sim10^{35}$ m$^{-3}$, then $P\propto n^{5/3}$ turns into $n^{4/3}$
links.regime: Same formula as long as $T\ll T_F$ and the electrons are non-relativistic ($E_F\ll m_ec^2=511$ keV). Copper: $n=8.5\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, $E_F=7.0$ eV, $k_BT/E_F=3.7\times10^{-3}$ at 300 K. A $0.6\,M_\odot$ white dwarf of radius $0.0125\,R_\odot$: $n_e\approx1.3\times10^{35}$ m$^{-3}$, $E_F\approx 94$ keV, $k_B(10^4\text{ K})/E_F\approx10^{-5}$.
links.experiment: In metals the degeneracy pressure shows up in the bulk modulus and in the electronic contribution to cohesion (order $10^{10}$ Pa); in white dwarfs it is measured through the mass-radius relation (Sirius B, $M\approx1\,M_\odot$, $R\approx0.008\,R_\odot$).
links.intuition: Pauli pressure is the same quantum kinetic energy per electron in both; what differs is the "container": electrostatics in the solid, gravity in the star. The density is $10^6$ times higher in the star, so $E_F$ is $10^4$ times larger.
links.exam: Degenerate Matter boss: cross-course Fermi gas.
links.why: Pauli pressure is the same quantum kinetic energy per electron in both; what differs is the "container": electrostatics in the solid, gravity in the star. The density is $10^6$ times higher in the star, so $E_F$ is $10^4$ times larger.

links.title: Metals and white dwarfs

sideA.context: Solid state: Fermi gas with $E_F\ll m_ec^2$, non-relativistic ($p=\hbar k$)

sideB.context: Astro: white dwarf with hydrostatic equilibrium $P\sim GM^2/R^4$ and $n\propto M/R^3$

map: $P\propto n^{4/3}\propto M^{4/3}/R^4$, the same $R^{-4}$ as the gravity requirement $GM^2/R^4$: $R$ cancels, and only one mass $M_{Ch}$ balances
links.regime: The $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ law holds for $0.1\lesssim M/M_\odot\lesssim0.8$ (non-relativistic). Near $1\,M_\odot$ the electrons become relativistic ($p_Fc\sim m_ec^2$), the radius shrinks faster, and $R\to0$ at $M_{Ch}$ (with $\mu_e=2$: $5.83/4=1.46$, quoted as about $1.4$).
links.experiment: Mass-radius relation from binary white dwarfs and Gaia parallaxes: more massive dwarfs are smaller. Sirius B has about $1\,M_\odot$ in the volume of the Earth.
links.intuition: Gravity wants to compress the star; Pauli pressure grows as $n^{5/3}$ and so wins at some radius. When electrons are ultra-relativistic the pressure only grows as $n^{4/3}$, the same scaling as gravity, so a critical mass appears.
links.exam: Degenerate Matter room: $R(M)$ and Chandrasekhar mass.
links.tex: P=K_{\rm NR}\,n^{5/3},\quad K_{\rm NR}=\frac{(3\pi^2)^{2/3}\hbar^2}{5m_e}\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ R\propto M^{-1/3};\quad P=K_{\rm UR}\,n^{4/3}\ \Rightarrow\ M_{Ch}=\frac{5.83}{\mu_e^2}M_\odot\approx1.46\,M_\odot
links.why: Gravity wants to compress the star; Pauli pressure grows as $n^{5/3}$ and so wins at some radius. When electrons are ultra-relativistic the pressure only grows as $n^{4/3}$, the same scaling as gravity, so a critical mass appears.

links.title: Uncertainty holds up a star

sideA.context: QM: confinement to size $\Delta x$ costs momentum spread $\Delta p\ge\hbar/2\Delta x$

sideB.context: Astro: $N$ electrons in a star of radius $R$ ($\Delta x\sim R/N^{1/3}$), gravity from the baryons $M=Nm_p$

map: Fermi momentum $p_F\sim\hbar n^{1/3}$ (Pauli: one electron per $h^3$ of phase space)
links.regime: An order-of-magnitude argument: the numerical factor is not $\hbar/2$-exact (Fermi gas gives $\tfrac35E_F$ per electron and $-\tfrac35GM^2/R$). For $N=M_\odot/m_p=1.2\times10^{57}$, $R_0\approx6\times10^6$ m, close to real white dwarfs ($\sim7\times10^6$ m).
links.experiment: The prediction $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ follows from $R_0\propto N^{-1/3}$; white-dwarf radii of order Earth radius are observed.
links.intuition: Squeeze electrons into a smaller volume and uncertainty forces them to move faster, the cost grows as $1/R^2$ and beats gravity's $1/R$ at small $R$, giving a minimum of $E(R)$.
links.exam: Fermi-estimate quick fights on white dwarf size.
links.why: Squeeze electrons into a smaller volume and uncertainty forces them to move faster, the cost grows as $1/R^2$ and beats gravity's $1/R$ at small $R$, giving a minimum of $E(R)$.

links.title: The size of the atom from uncertainty

sideA.context: QM: one electron confined within radius $r$, $p\sim\hbar/r$

sideB.context: Hydrogen: exact Schroedinger solution of the Coulomb problem

links.regime: The heuristic with $p=\hbar/r$ happens to give the exact ground state; in general only the scaling is trustworthy (factors of order 1). It works for the ground state, not for excited states ($n>1$), where nodes matter.
links.experiment: The atomic size $\sim\text{\AA}$ and the binding energy $\sim10$ eV are measured by ionisation and X-ray scattering; Lyman limit at 91.2 nm.
links.intuition: The atom is stable because squeezing the electron toward the nucleus costs kinetic energy $\propto1/r^2$ faster than the Coulomb gain $\propto1/r$.
links.why: The atom is stable because squeezing the electron toward the nucleus costs kinetic energy $\propto1/r^2$ faster than the Coulomb gain $\propto1/r$.

links.title: Every normal mode is an oscillator

sideA.context: Solid state: monatomic chain, lattice constant $a$, spring constant $C$, mass $M$, normal-mode wave vector $q$

sideB.context: QM: harmonic oscillator of frequency $\omega$ with ladder operators

map: one independent oscillator with $\omega=\omega_s(q)$ (after diagonalising the coupled system)
number of phonons in the mode: $E=\sum_{q,s}\hbar\omega_s(q)(n_{q,s}+\tfrac12)$
phonon creation and annihilation operators; bosons, so any $n$ allowed
$\tfrac12\hbar\omega$ per mode remains at $T=0$ (zero-point motion of the lattice)
links.regime: Exact in the harmonic approximation. Anharmonic terms (thermal expansion, finite phonon lifetimes) couple the modes and break it. A typical phonon of $\omega\approx10^{13}$ rad/s has $\hbar\omega\approx6.6$ meV, which corresponds to $T\approx76$ K and sets the scale of $\Theta_D$.
links.experiment: Inelastic neutron scattering measures $\omega(q)$ and the creation/annihilation of single phonons ($\hbar\omega\sim$ meV to tens of meV). The Einstein heat capacity is just $N$ copies of the oscillator thermal average.
links.intuition: A crystal is $3N$ uncoupled quantum oscillators after the change to normal coordinates; "phonon" is the name for one quantum $\hbar\omega$ of such a mode.
links.exam: Phonon Halls: Einstein vs Debye; elevator: ladder operators.
links.why: A crystal is $3N$ uncoupled quantum oscillators after the change to normal coordinates; "phonon" is the name for one quantum $\hbar\omega$ of such a mode.

links.title: Debye $T^3$ and Stefan-Boltzmann $T^4$

sideA.context: Solid state: phonon gas at $T\ll\Theta_D$, linear dispersion $\omega=vq$, 3 polarisations (1 longitudinal, 2 transverse)

sideB.context: Astro: photon gas in a cavity (blackbody), $\omega=ck$, 2 polarisations

map: no cutoff: infinitely many modes, hence $U\propto T^4$ at all $T$
links.regime: Phonons follow $T^3$ only for $T\ll\Theta_D$ (rule of thumb $T\lesssim\Theta_D/50$); above the cutoff all $3N$ modes are filled and $C\to3Nk_B$ (Dulong-Petit). Photons have no cutoff. Copper ($\Theta_D=343$ K) at 10 K: $C/Nk_B=\tfrac{12\pi^4}{5}(T/\Theta_D)^3\approx5.8\times10^{-3}$. Radiation constant $a=7.566\times10^{-16}$ J m$^{-3}$K$^{-4}$.
links.experiment: Low-temperature heat capacities of insulators follow $C=\beta T^3$ over decades; the blackbody spectrum of the CMB or of the Sun follows $T^4$, so $F=\sigma T^4$ with $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W m$^{-2}$K$^{-4}$.
links.intuition: Both are a gas of massless bosons with $\mu=0$ and linear dispersion; they differ only in the speed, the polarisation count and the Debye cutoff that a lattice must have.
links.exam: Heat-capacity problems (Debye law) and blackbody problems share the integral $\int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x-1)\,dx=\pi^4/15$.
links.why: Both are a gas of massless bosons with $\mu=0$ and linear dispersion; they differ only in the speed, the polarisation count and the Debye cutoff that a lattice must have.

links.title: Hund's rules and the Lande factor

sideA.context: Solid state: ion with total $\mathbf J=\mathbf L+\mathbf S$ (Hund's rules, LS coupling), paramagnet at high $T$

sideB.context: QM: addition of two angular momenta, coupled basis $|J,M\rangle$ built from $|L,m_L\rangle|S,m_S\rangle$ with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients

map: allowed total angular momentum of the coupled pair, the lowest/highest by Hund's third rule
links.regime: Valid for rare-earth ions (4f electrons well shielded, spin-orbit coupling $\gg$ crystal field) at temperatures where only the ground $J$-multiplet is populated. For 3d ions the crystal field quenches $L$ and $\mu_{\rm eff}\approx g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B$ fits better.
links.experiment: The Curie constant $C=\mu_0N\mu_{\rm eff}^2/3k_B$ is read from the slope of $1/\chi(T)$; Gd$^{3+}$ salts give $7.9\,\mu_B$ as predicted from the spin-only sum.
links.intuition: Hund's rules tell you which $|L,S,J\rangle$ multiplet is lowest; the Clebsch-Gordan/projection machinery gives the magnetic moment of that coupled state.
links.why: Hund's rules tell you which $|L,S,J\rangle$ multiplet is lowest; the Clebsch-Gordan/projection machinery gives the magnetic moment of that coupled state.

links.title: Spin-1/2 in a field is a magnet

sideA.context: Solid state: independent localised moments $\mu=\tfrac12g\mu_B$ in field $B$ at temperature $T$ (Langevin, $J=\tfrac12$)

sideB.context: QM: spin-1/2 with $g=2$ in $\mathbf B=B\hat z$

map: two Zeeman levels with Boltzmann weights $e^{\mp\mu_BB/k_BT}$
electron spin resonance frequency, $28$ GHz per T
links.regime: Free-spin Curie law needs $k_BT\gg\mu_BB$ and no interaction. At 1 T, $\mu_BB/k_B=0.67$ K, so at 300 K the polarisation is only $\tanh(2.2\times10^{-3})\approx2\times10^{-3}$. Interactions give Curie-Weiss $\chi\propto1/(T-\Theta)$.
links.experiment: SQUID magnetometry of $\chi(T)$ and electron spin resonance at $\approx28$ GHz/T are direct measurements of this two-level splitting.
links.intuition: A paramagnet is a statistical ensemble of Stern-Gerlach spins: each moment is a two-level quantum system; only the Boltzmann populations of the two levels are new.
links.tex: M=n\mu_B\tanh\frac{\mu_BB}{k_BT}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mu_BB\ll k_BT\ }\ \chi=\frac{\mu_0n\mu_B^2}{k_BT}\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ H=g\mu_B\,\frac{\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B}{\hbar}=\mu_BB\,\sigma_z,\quad E_\pm=\pm\mu_BB
links.why: A paramagnet is a statistical ensemble of Stern-Gerlach spins: each moment is a two-level quantum system; only the Boltzmann populations of the two levels are new.

links.title: Electron waves diffract: Bragg and de Broglie

sideA.context: Solid state: scattering of waves from a crystal with lattice planes of spacing $d$

sideB.context: QM: free particle of momentum $\mathbf p$ has plane-wave state $e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}$

map: crystal momentum conservation: $\mathbf k'=\mathbf k+\mathbf G$, elastic: $|\mathbf k'|=|\mathbf k|$
links.regime: Diffraction needs $\lambda\lesssim2d$ (Bragg condition has a solution). Electrons of 54 eV have $\lambda=1.67$ Å, comparable to atomic spacing; thermal neutrons (25 meV) have 1.8 Å; X-rays of 8 keV have 1.5 Åbut different scattering mechanism (charge density).
links.experiment: Davisson-Germer 1927: 54 eV electrons on Ni(111), peak at $\varphi=50^\circ$, and $d\sin\varphi=2.15\,\text{\AA}\cdot0.766=1.65$ Åversus the de Broglie prediction $1.67$ Å.
links.intuition: Matter waves interfere on a crystal exactly like X-rays: the periodic potential only allows momentum changes of $\hbar\mathbf G$, which is why the diffraction pattern is a map of the reciprocal lattice.
links.why: Matter waves interfere on a crystal exactly like X-rays: the periodic potential only allows momentum changes of $\hbar\mathbf G$, which is why the diffraction pattern is a map of the reciprocal lattice.

links.title: Pauli paramagnetism from Zeeman perturbation

sideA.context: Metals: free-electron gas with $T\ll T_F$ in a small field $B$

sideB.context: QM: first-order perturbation theory for a spin-1/2 electron, $H'=\pm\mu_BB$

map: first-order energy shifts of the two spin states
excess of one spin direction $\delta n=\tfrac12\nu(E_F)\mu_BB$ per volume
electrons near $E_F$ flip to the lower-energy spin band (only a shell of width $\mu_BB$ below $E_F$ can)
replaces the classical Curie factor $1/k_BT$: effective $k_BT\to E_F$
links.regime: Valid for $\mu_BB\ll E_F$ (always, $\mu_BB\sim0.06$ meV at 1 T) and $T\ll T_F$. Compared with free moments (Curie), the susceptibility is reduced by $\sim k_BT/E_F\sim10^{-2}$ and is temperature independent. Na ($n=2.65\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, $E_F=3.24$ eV): $\chi_P\approx8.3\times10^{-6}$ (SI).
links.experiment: Susceptibility of simple metals (Na, K) is of order $10^{-5}$ and nearly $T$-independent; it also enters in Knight-shift NMR. Landau diamagnetism of the electron gas subtracts $-\tfrac13\chi_P$.
links.intuition: Spins lower their energy in the field, but the Pauli principle forbids flipping any electron deep in the sea, so only the small fraction $\sim\mu_BB/E_F$ near the Fermi surface responds.
links.why: Spins lower their energy in the field, but the Pauli principle forbids flipping any electron deep in the sea, so only the small fraction $\sim\mu_BB/E_F$ near the Fermi surface responds.

links.title: A donor is a hydrogen atom in a crystal

sideA.context: Solid state: shallow donor (P in Si, Si in GaAs) with effective mass $m^*$ in a dielectric of relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$

sideB.context: QM: hydrogen atom, electron mass $m_e$ in vacuum

map: $\epsilon_r\epsilon_0$ (static screening by the lattice, $\epsilon_r=12.9$ for GaAs)
links.regime: Valid when $a_d\gg a_{\rm lattice}$ (effective-mass theory, slowly varying envelope) and the carrier sits at a band edge with isotropic parabolic $E(k)$. In Si the anisotropic mass and central-cell corrections give 45 meV for P instead of the 26 meV hydrogenic estimate; the hydrogenic series $E_n\propto1/n^2$ is seen for excited donor states.
links.experiment: Far-infrared absorption shows the donor Lyman series (1s to 2p) at meV energies; carriers freeze out below $T\sim E_d/k_B\approx64$ K in GaAs ($5.5$ meV), above it all donors are ionised, giving $n=N_d$ (extrinsic regime).
links.intuition: The electron orbits the ionised donor like in hydrogen, but the lattice makes it light ($m^*$) and screens the Coulomb force ($\epsilon_r$), so the atom is $10^3$ times bigger and $10^3$ times more weakly bound.
links.exam: Semiconductor Forge: "A hydrogen atom in a crystal: the donor".
links.why: The electron orbits the ionised donor like in hydrogen, but the lattice makes it light ($m^*$) and screens the Coulomb force ($\epsilon_r$), so the atom is $10^3$ times bigger and $10^3$ times more weakly bound.

links.title: Drude conduction and photon diffusion

sideA.context: Solid state: electrons scattering with mean free time $\tau$ and mean free path $\ell=v_F\tau$ in a metal

sideB.context: Astro: photons scattering in a stellar interior with mean free path $\ell=1/(\kappa\rho)$

map: random walk of electrons between collisions
random walk of photons: $N=(R/\ell)^2$ steps, time $N\ell/c$
links.regime: Both need $\ell\ll$ system size (diffusive, not ballistic). Cu at 300 K: $\tau\approx2.5\times10^{-14}$ s, $v_F=1.57\times10^6$ m/s, $\ell\approx39$ nm, $\sigma\approx6\times10^7$ S/m. Solar centre: $\kappa\approx1$ cm$^2$/g, $\rho\approx1.5\times10^5$ kg/m$^3$, $\ell\approx0.07$ mm, so a photon needs $\sim8\times10^5$ yr to leave. (Estimates with a larger $\ell$, e.g. 1 cm, give $5\times10^3$ yr.)
links.experiment: Ohm's law and Wiedemann-Franz relate $\sigma$ to $\kappa_{\rm th}$ in metals; in the Sun the photons made at the core arrive as sunlight after $10^4$ to $10^6$ yr, while neutrinos arrive after 8 minutes.
links.intuition: Frequent collisions turn directed motion into diffusion with $D\sim v\ell$. Same random-walk logic, but electrons carry charge (drift in $E$ field), photons carry energy (drift down a temperature gradient).
links.tex: \sigma=\frac{ne^2\tau}{m},\quad D=\tfrac13 v_F\ell\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ t_{\rm diff}\approx\frac{R^2}{\ell c},\quad D=\tfrac13c\,\ell
links.why: Frequent collisions turn directed motion into diffusion with $D\sim v\ell$. Same random-walk logic, but electrons carry charge (drift in $E$ field), photons carry energy (drift down a temperature gradient).

links.title: The 21 cm line is $\tfrac12\otimes\tfrac12=0\oplus1$

sideA.context: Astro: neutral hydrogen in the ISM, electron and proton spin in the 1s ground state

sideB.context: QM: addition of two spins-1/2 with $H=A\,\mathbf I\cdot\mathbf S/\hbar^2$

links.regime: The $3{:}1$ population ratio holds whenever the spin temperature $T_S\gg h\nu/k=0.068$ K, which is true almost everywhere (collisions, Lyman-$\alpha$ pumping). The line is optically thin in most directions, so intensity $\propto N_{HI}$. Very forbidden: only the huge column densities of the ISM make it visible.
links.experiment: Radio telescopes map HI (spiral arms, rotation curves via Doppler shift of 21 cm), Zeeman splitting gives $B$ in the ISM; the Epoch of Reionization uses it at redshift.
links.intuition: The magnetic interaction between the two spins only distinguishes total spin 1 (parallel) from 0 (antiparallel); the difference is tiny, $5.9\ \mu$eV, so the photon wavelength is 21 cm.
links.exam: Angular-momentum addition exercises; ISM column density.
links.why: The magnetic interaction between the two spins only distinguishes total spin 1 (parallel) from 0 (antiparallel); the difference is tiny, $5.9\ \mu$eV, so the photon wavelength is 21 cm.

links.title: Absorption lines are hydrogen transitions

sideA.context: Astro: stellar atmosphere in LTE, level populations of H at temperature $T$ (Boltzmann, Saha)

sideB.context: QM: hydrogen levels $E_n=-\mathrm{Ry}/n^2$ and transitions $n\to m$

map: Balmer absorption needs atoms in $n=2$, i.e. $10.2$ eV above the ground state
links.regime: In LTE the fraction of atoms in $n=2$ at $T=10^4$ K is only $4e^{-11.8}\approx3\times10^{-5}$ ($k_BT=0.86$ eV), but at the same time ionisation (Saha) depletes H; the product peaks at about $9{,}500$ K, which is why Balmer lines are strongest in A stars and weaker in hotter or cooler stars.
links.experiment: The spectral type sequence OBAFGKM is a temperature sequence read from line strengths: He II (O), Balmer (A), Ca II (F/G), molecules (M). Hα at $656.3$ nm in air is the standard hydrogen line.
links.intuition: Quantum mechanics gives the wavelengths (where the lines are), statistical mechanics plus radiative transfer give how deep they are (how many atoms in the right level).
links.why: Quantum mechanics gives the wavelengths (where the lines are), statistical mechanics plus radiative transfer give how deep they are (how many atoms in the right level).

links.title: Planck spectrum from standing waves

sideA.context: Astro: blackbody specific intensity of a star or the CMB

sideB.context: QM: standing waves in a box, energy of a mode $\hbar\omega$ per quantum

map: thermal average gives the Planck factor (see harmonic oscillator)
links.regime: Holds in thermal equilibrium (cavity, optically thick source). Stars are approximate blackbodies; the Sun at $T_{\rm eff}=5772$ K peaks at $502$ nm (Wien in wavelength). The CMB at $2.725$ K is the best blackbody measured.
links.experiment: Fitting $B_\lambda(T)$ to a spectrum gives $T_{\rm eff}$; with the flux $F=\sigma T^4$ and luminosity this gives the radius $R=\sqrt{L/4\pi\sigma T^4}$.
links.intuition: Quantised standing waves give a finite number of modes per frequency, quantised energy suppresses high-frequency modes ($h\nu\gg k_BT$), which cures the ultraviolet catastrophe.
links.why: Quantised standing waves give a finite number of modes per frequency, quantised energy suppresses high-frequency modes ($h\nu\gg k_BT$), which cures the ultraviolet catastrophe.

links.title: The CMB is a redshifted blackbody

sideA.context: Astro: blackbody of temperature $T$, photon number density

sideB.context: Cosmology: expansion with scale factor $a$ and redshift $1+z=a_0/a$

map: stretched by $a$: $\lambda_{\max}$ moves from about $1\ \mu$m to $1.06$ mm

links.title: The virial theorem from stars to clusters

sideA.context: Stars: self-gravitating gas ball in hydrostatic equilibrium, $K$ thermal energy

sideB.context: Galaxies: collisionless system of stars with velocity dispersion $\sigma$ (1D)

map: same $U$; actual profile changes the factor of order 1
velocity dispersion $\sigma^2$ plays the role of $k_BT/m$

links.title: The Eddington limit for stars and quasars

sideA.context: Stars: radiation pressure on electrons vs gravity on protons, Thomson scattering $\sigma_T=6.65\times10^{-29}$ m$^2$

sideB.context: AGN: accretion onto a supermassive black hole, luminosity from infall

map: mass $M_{\rm BH}$ of the black hole
links.regime: Spherical, fully ionised hydrogen, steady state, opacity from Thomson scattering. Stars above $\sim100\,M_\odot$ approach $L_{\rm Edd}$ and lose mass in winds; AGN can be super-Eddington only briefly or non-spherically.
links.experiment: Quasar luminosities $10^{38}$ to $10^{40}$ W imply black holes of $10^8$ to $10^9M_\odot$ if they radiate near Eddington.
links.intuition: Same balance in both: outward momentum of the light per unit time against inward gravity. The limit scales with $M$ and not with radius because both forces fall as $r^{-2}$.
links.tex: L_{\rm Edd}=\frac{4\pi GMm_pc}{\sigma_T}=3.3\times10^4\Big(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\Big)L_\odot\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ L=\eta\dot Mc^2\le L_{\rm Edd},\quad \eta\approx0.1

links.title: Reaction rates against expansion: BBN

sideA.context: Astro: weak interactions interconverting $n\leftrightarrow p$ in equilibrium

sideB.context: Cosmology: freeze-out when the interaction rate $\Gamma$ falls below the Hubble rate $H$

map: $n/p\approx0.2$ at freeze-out ($k_BT\approx0.8$ MeV), $\approx1/7$ after neutron decay
all neutrons end in $^4$He: $Y_p=2x/(1+x)$ with $x=1/7$ gives $0.25$
links.regime: Equilibrium requires $\Gamma\gg H$. After freeze-out only free neutron decay ($\tau_n=880$ s) changes $n/p$ until deuterium forms at $k_BT\approx0.07$ MeV, since the photon-to-baryon ratio ($\sim10^9$) delays deuterium by photodissociation.
links.experiment: Observed primordial helium abundance $Y_p=0.245\pm0.003$ and deuterium $D/H\approx2.5\times10^{-5}$ fix the baryon density.
links.intuition: Nuclear physics (Q-values, Boltzmann factors) in a fire that cools: whichever reaction is faster than expansion stays in equilibrium, the rest freezes.
links.tex: \frac nP=e^{-\Delta m c^2/k_BT},\quad \Delta mc^2=1.293\text{ MeV}\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ \Gamma(T)\sim H(T)\propto T^2\ \Rightarrow\ Y_p=\frac{2(n/p)}{1+n/p}\approx0.25
links.why: Nuclear physics (Q-values, Boltzmann factors) in a fire that cools: whichever reaction is faster than expansion stays in equilibrium, the rest freezes.

links.title: Enclosed mass and the Friedmann equation

sideA.context: Galaxies: circular orbit, mass enclosed by shell theorem

sideB.context: Cosmology: test particle at comoving radius $r=a\chi$ in a uniform sphere of density $\rho$

map: same shell theorem for a homogeneous sphere
closed universe $k=+1$; $E=0$ gives critical density $\rho_c=3H^2/8\pi G$
links.regime: Newtonian derivation reproduces Friedmann for matter-only (pressure-free) universes; it fails for radiation and for $\Lambda$ without GR. links.intuition: Both use the shell theorem: only mass inside the radius matters; orbits vs expansion are the same gravitational dynamics with different initial velocities.

links.title: Anharmonic oscillator with ladder operators

sideA.context: QM: oscillator with $x=\sqrt{\hbar/2m\omega}\,(a+a^\dagger)$

sideB.context: Perturbation theory: $H=H_0+\lambda x^4$

map: make the matrix elements of $H'$ calculable by counting the paths of raising/lowering
links.regime: First order is valid for $E^{(1)}\ll\hbar\omega$, i.e. $\lambda\hbar/m^2\omega^3\ll1$; higher $n$ makes it worse because $E^{(1)}\propto n^2$. For the quartic oscillator the perturbation series is asymptotic, not convergent.
links.experiment: Level spacing of anharmonic vibrations of molecules (overtones are not exactly at $n\omega$) and thermal expansion of crystals.
links.intuition: Ladder operators turn each position operator into $a+a^\dagger$, so every perturbation theory integral becomes an algebraic count.

links.title: Zeeman splitting of hydrogen lines

sideA.context: QM: orbital angular momentum $l$, magnetic moment $-\mu_B\mathbf L/\hbar$ in field $B$

sideB.context: Hydrogen lamp: Balmer line H$\alpha$ in a magnetic field

links.regime: Normal Zeeman applies when spin is zero or when $\mu_BB\gg$ spin-orbit (Paschen-Back); in weak fields with spin-orbit, $g_J$ weights. For H $n=2$, fine structure is $4.5\times10^{-5}$ eV, comparable to $\mu_BB$ at $0.8$ T.

links.intuition: The magnetic field lifts the $m$-degeneracy of the level: each $m$ gets its own energy, and the emitted photons have the polarisation fixed by $\Delta m$.

links.title: The singlet is the entangled state

sideA.context: Two spins-1/2 coupled to total spin $S=0$

sideB.context: Measurement of spin along $\hat a$ and $\hat b$ on the two particles
sideB.tex: E(\hat a,\hat b)=-\hat a\cdot\hat b=-\cos\theta,\quad S_{\rm CHSH}=2\sqrt2

map: maximally entangled pair, not a product of single-particle states
perfect anticorrelation along any common axis
amplitudes of the Bell state; they cannot factor
links.regime: Holds for ideal projective measurements and no decoherence. Local hidden variable theories satisfy $|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2$; the singlet reaches $2\sqrt2=2.83$ for suitable angles.
links.experiment: Aspect 1982 and loophole-free tests (2015) measure $S\approx2.4$ to $2.8$ with photon or electron pairs.
links.intuition: The Clebsch-Gordan decomposition makes the singlet's anticorrelation automatic; entanglement is a property of that coupled state.
links.tex: |0,0\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\big(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle\big)\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ E(\hat a,\hat b)=-\hat a\cdot\hat b=-\cos\theta,\quad S_{\rm CHSH}=2\sqrt2
links.why: The Clebsch-Gordan decomposition makes the singlet's anticorrelation automatic; entanglement is a property of that coupled state.

links.title: Fine structure as first-order perturbation

sideA.context: Hydrogen with relativistic and spin-orbit corrections

sideB.context: Degenerate perturbation theory: diagonalise $H'$ in the degenerate subspace
sideB.tex: \langle n l j m_j|H'|n l' j' m_j'\rangle\ \text{diagonal in the coupled basis}

map: splits into $2p_{3/2}$ and $2p_{1/2}$ (and $2s_{1/2}$ degenerate with $2p_{1/2}$ at this order)
$j$, $m_j$ (since $\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf S$ commutes with $J^2$, not with $L_z,S_z$)
links.regime: Valid for $H'\ll$ level spacing; relative size $\alpha^2/n^2\approx5\times10^{-5}$ for $n=1$. It needs the right basis: $|n,l,m_l,m_s\rangle$ would give wrong results because $H'$ is not diagonal there.

links.intuition: Perturbation theory is only meaningful in the basis that diagonalises the perturbation inside each degenerate level.
links.tex: E_{nj}^{(1)}=E_n\,\frac{\alpha^2}{n^2}\Big(\frac{n}{j+1/2}-\frac34\Big)\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ \langle n l j m_j|H'|n l' j' m_j'\rangle\ \text{diagonal in the coupled basis}
links.why: Perturbation theory is only meaningful in the basis that diagonalises the perturbation inside each degenerate level.

links.title: Only a thin shell of electrons carries heat

sideA.context: Metals: Sommerfeld heat capacity of the degenerate electron gas, $T\ll T_F$

sideB.context: White dwarf interior: electron gas with $T\ll T_F$ inside a classical ion gas

map: $T_F=E_F/k_B$ of the metal ($8.2\times10^4$ K for Cu)
fraction $T/T_F$ of electrons that can absorb heat
same fraction, so the electrons are a heat-less pressure source and the ions store the heat
links.regime: Requires $T\ll T_F$ (Pauli blocking: only states within $k_BT$ of $E_F$ can be excited). For Cu at 300 K only $0.6\%$ of the Dulong-Petit value $3Nk_B$ comes from electrons; it dominates below $\sim4$ K. In a white dwarf the cooling is controlled by the ions (heat capacity) and by the thin non-degenerate envelope.
links.experiment: Cu: $\gamma\approx0.7$ mJ/(mol K$^2$) from low-$T$ calorimetry. White-dwarf cooling curves (luminosity function of the Galactic disc) give ages up to $\sim10$ Gyr.
links.intuition: Pauli blocking prevents most electrons from taking up energy; the same Fermi surface constraint sets both the metallic heat capacity and the slow cooling of dead stars.
links.why: Pauli blocking prevents most electrons from taking up energy; the same Fermi surface constraint sets both the metallic heat capacity and the slow cooling of dead stars.

links.title: A covalent bond is a split double well

sideA.context: Solid state: two atoms with orbitals $|a\rangle$, $|b\rangle$ and overlap/transfer integral $t=-\langle a|H|b\rangle$

sideB.context: QM: a particle in a symmetric double well, barrier of width $d$ between the minima

map: even ground state of the double well
proportional to the barrier tunnelling amplitude $\propto e^{-\kappa d}$
balance of $t(R)$ (decreasing with distance) against ion-ion repulsion
links.regime: Two-level (tight-binding) approximation holds when the splitting is small compared to the other level spacings, $t\ll\hbar\omega$, and $\kappa d\gg1$. Simple LCAO for H$_2^+$: $D_e=1.76$ eV at $R_e=2.49\,a_0$, while the exact value is $2.79$ eV at $2.00\,a_0$.
links.experiment: Ammonia inversion: the N atom tunnels between two sides of the H$_3$ plane, splitting $h\times23.79$ GHz $=98$ $\mu$eV (maser line). In solids, $N$ coupled wells give a band of width $4t$.
links.intuition: Tunnelling lets the electron be in both wells at once; the symmetric combination has no node between them and is lower, giving the bond. The exponential sensitivity to distance is why bonds are short-ranged.
links.tex: E_\pm=\epsilon_0\mp t,\quad |\pm\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|a\rangle\pm|b\rangle)\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ \Delta E=E_{\rm odd}-E_{\rm even}=2t\sim\hbar\omega\,e^{-\kappa d}
links.why: Tunnelling lets the electron be in both wells at once; the symmetric combination has no node between them and is lower, giving the bond. The exponential sensitivity to distance is why bonds are short-ranged.

links.title: LCAO: building molecules from hydrogen orbitals

sideA.context: Solid state: LCAO ansatz $\psi=c_a\phi_a+c_b\phi_b$ for two identical atoms, overlap $S=\langle\phi_a|\phi_b\rangle$

sideB.context: QM: hydrogen 1s orbital $\phi=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi a_0^3}}e^{-r/a_0}$, $E_{1s}=-13.6$ eV

map: $E_{1s}$ plus Coulomb integral to the other nucleus
exchange (resonance) integral, negative because the orbitals overlap in the attractive region
links.regime: Works best for small overlap and for atoms whose valence orbitals are hydrogen-like (s orbitals). The LCAO H$_2^+$ binding energy $1.76$ eV at $R_e=2.49\,a_0$ underestimates the exact $2.79$ eV; adding a variational exponent improves it.
links.experiment: Molecular spectroscopy of H$_2$ and H$_2^+$: $D_0(\mathrm{H}_2)=4.52$ eV, $R_e=0.74$ Å, with vibrational quanta $\hbar\omega\approx0.52$ eV.
links.intuition: Atomic orbitals from the hydrogen problem are the basis functions; the bond forms because the electron can be shared, lowering the kinetic energy.
links.tex: E_\pm=\frac{H_{aa}\pm H_{ab}}{1\pm S},\quad H_{ab}<0\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ S=e^{-R/a_0}\Big(1+\frac R{a_0}+\frac{R^2}{3a_0^2}\Big)

links.title: Degenerate metal versus Boltzmann semiconductor

sideA.context: Metal: Fermi-Dirac occupation with $E_F\gg k_BT$, $\mu\approx E_F$ inside the band

sideB.context: Semiconductor: $\mu$ in the gap, $E_c-\mu\gg k_BT$, non-degenerate

map: reduces to the Boltzmann factor $e^{-(E-\mu)/k_BT}$ when $E-\mu\gg k_BT$
$\mu$ at mid-gap for intrinsic material (up to $\tfrac34k_BT\ln(m_h^*/m_e^*)$)
links.regime: Boltzmann statistics need $n\ll N_c$. Si at 300 K: $E_g=1.12$ eV, $k_BT=25.9$ meV, $e^{-E_g/2k_BT}=3.9\times10^{-10}$, so $n_i\approx10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$, $13$ orders below Cu's $8.5\times10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$. Heavy doping ($>10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$) makes a semiconductor degenerate and metallic.
links.experiment: Resistivity of Cu rises weakly with $T$ (more scattering), that of Si falls exponentially with $T$; the slope of $\ln\sigma$ vs $1/T$ gives $E_g/2$.
links.intuition: The same distribution: in a metal the Fermi sea fills it up to $E_F$, in a semiconductor the chemical potential lies in the gap and only the exponential tail reaches the band.

links.why: The same distribution: in a metal the Fermi sea fills it up to $E_F$, in a semiconductor the chemical potential lies in the gap and only the exponential tail reaches the band.

links.title: Bloch theorem is a commuting operator

sideA.context: Solid state: periodic potential $V(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=V(\mathbf r)$, eigenstates labelled by crystal momentum $\mathbf k$
sideA.tex: \psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)

sideB.context: QM: translation operator and commuting observables

map: $[H,T_{\mathbf R}]=0$ for lattice vectors only, not for all translations
unit-modulus eigenvalue of unitary $T$; $k$ is defined only mod $2\pi/a$
links.regime: Exact for an infinite perfect periodic lattice. Crystal momentum $\hbar k$ is not the momentum $\langle p\rangle$ because $[p,T]\neq0$ when $V$ is only discretely periodic. For Cu (fcc, $a=3.61$ Å) the zone boundary along the cube edge is $\pi/a=0.87$ Å$^{-1}$, where a free electron has $\hbar^2k^2/2m=2.9$ eV.

links.intuition: A symmetry gives a conserved quantity; for a lattice the symmetry is discrete, so the conserved quantity ($k$) is only defined up to reciprocal lattice vectors.
links.tex: \psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)\ \ \leftrightarrow\ \ T_a=e^{-i\hat pa/\hbar},\quad[H,T_a]=0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{common eigenstates},\ T_a\psi=e^{-ika}\psi
links.why: A symmetry gives a conserved quantity; for a lattice the symmetry is discrete, so the conserved quantity ($k$) is only defined up to reciprocal lattice vectors.

links.title: Kinetic conduction: phonons and photons

sideA.context: Solid state: thermal conductivity of a phonon gas with heat capacity $C$ (per volume), speed $v$, mean free path $\ell$

sideB.context: Stars: radiative conductivity of a photon gas, $C_{\rm rad}=4aT^3$, speed $c$, $\ell=1/(\kappa\rho)$

map: low $T$: $\ell$ limited by sample size, $\kappa_{\rm th}\propto T^3$
energy flux $F=-K_{\rm rad}\,dT/dr=L/4\pi r^2$, so $dT/dr=-\frac{3\kappa\rho L}{16\pi acT^3r^2}$

links.title: Degeneracy removes the stellar thermostat: helium flash

sideA.context: Solid state / degenerate gas: pressure independent of temperature for $T\ll T_F$

sideB.context: Red-giant helium core with $\rho_c\approx10^9$ kg/m$^3$ and $T\approx10^8$ K, triple-alpha rate $\varepsilon_{3\alpha}\propto T^{\sim40}$

map: no negative feedback: normal stars expand when heated and cool, degenerate ones do not

links.experiment: Observationally the red-clump and horizontal-branch stars (post-flash) have nearly identical luminosity because the core mass at the flash is fixed ($0.47\,M_\odot$).
links.intuition: A stove with a throttle that cannot open: heat the degenerate gas and it cannot expand, so the energy goes into more burning.
